title: Vishvamitra takes the boys
hook: a king promises a visitor anything, then hears what he wants

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dasharatha's sacrifice, part three. Ravana scorned humans, and four sons were born. Did you let one overlooked thing count? Now the boys have grown. Day four hundred ninety-eight.
screen: `FOUR SONS, BORN TO ANSWER A BOAST.`

segments.voice: The four princes grow up learned, brave and close. Lakshmana sticks to Rama like a second shadow; Shatrughna to Bharata. Dasharatha, delighted, is already talking with his counselors about their weddings. Then a guard rushes in: the sage Vishvamitra is at the gate. Dasharatha hurries out to meet him, washes his feet, honors him, and says the words a king says to an honored guest, and maybe shouldn't: whatever you ask, consider it done. Vishvamitra smiles, and asks.
screen: `FOUR PRINCES, GROWN.` → `A FAMOUS SAGE AT THE GATE.` → `WHATEVER YOU ASK, IT'S DONE.`

segments.voice: Vishvamitra explains. He's begun a sacrifice, and two rakshasas, Maricha and Subahu, keep wrecking it, pouring blood and flesh on the altar. Under his vow he can't curse them in anger. So he asks for Rama. Give me your eldest son, the boy who still wears a child's side-locks, for ten nights, to guard my rite. And Dasharatha's world tilts. He nearly faints. Then he pleads, and Valmiki gives us his words: unashodasha-varsho me ramo rajivalochanah. My lotus-eyed Rama is not yet sixteen. He's never fought. Take my army instead. Take me. I'll fight them myself. And then, when he hears who stands behind Maricha and Subahu, he grows more frightened still: Ravana. No, not Rama. Now, who is Vishvamitra? He wasn't born a sage. He was born a king, a warrior who, the Ramayana tells later, spent ages of fierce austerity until he became a brahmarshi, a sage of the highest rank. His name means friend of the whole world. And he's famous for his fire. When Dasharatha takes back his promise, that fire rises. The sage says: you're breaking your word, king. Fine. I'll go as I came. And the whole earth, the text says, trembles. Under the noise of the scene is something quiet. A father who has promised his son away, and can't bear to let him go.
screen: `TWO RAKSHASAS RUIN HIS SACRIFICE.` · `RAMA IS NOT YET SIXTEEN.` · `A KING WHO BECAME A SAGE.` · `A PROMISE TAKEN BACK.` · then, large: `ŪNAṢOḌAŚAVARṢO ME RĀMO RĀJĪVALOCANAḤ.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Think of someone you love who is stepping into something bigger than you'd like: a child, a friend, a younger sibling, maybe your younger self. Notice if part of you wants to hold on. Don't argue with it. Then, on each breath out, loosen your grip by one finger. Not letting them go, just loosening. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer. The bell holds the time.
Vishvamitra takes the boys. The king-turned-sage asks Dasharatha for Rama to guard his sacrifice, and a father's promise meets a father's fear.
Your line: Vishvamitra takes the boys. Today, before you say whatever you want, it's yours, pause for one breath and ask what it might cost. Day four hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Vishvamitra is honored in Hindu tradition as one of the great rishis; the Gayatri mantra of the Rig Veda is traditionally credited to him, and his request for Rama is told as the moment the prince's life of service begins.

match.prompt: at Dasharatha's gate — tap the pairs.
pairs: a king who became a sage

myth: Vishvamitra was born a brahmin sage
he was born a king and became a brahmarshi through fierce austerity.
Dasharatha offers to fight the rakshasas himself
he offers his army, and himself, instead of Rama.
Vishvamitra curses the rakshasas instead of asking for help
under his vow he won't curse them in anger, so he asks for Rama.

fork.setup: you're Dasharatha. you promised the sage anything. he asks for your teenage son to fight rakshasas. what do you do?
options: plead, and offer yourself and your army instead.
fork.reveal: he pleads that Rama isn't yet sixteen and offers to go himself. Vishvamitra, angered at a broken promise, makes to leave.

original.note: Sanskrit viśvāmitra: viśva (all, the whole world) + mitra (friend).

trapdoor: what you thought: Dasharatha simply lends Rama to a sage.
what it means: he's caught between a promise and his fear for his son, and he breaks down.

what a scholar hears: Bala Kanda 18–20 set the scene; Dasharatha's line unashodasha-varsho, less than sixteen, is often cited for Rama's age; Vishvamitra's own rise from king to brahmarshi is told later by Shatananda.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 18–21 (Vishvamitra's arrival, request and anger)
Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 51–65 (Vishvamitra's life, told by Shatananda)

notes: Verse 20.2 follows a common vulgate numbering; confirm the line and number.
'Ten days' for the sacrifice: the text speaks of ten nights (dasharatra); confirm.
'The one with curly hair' (kakapaksha-dhara) paraphrased; confirm.
Gayatri mantra credited to Vishvamitra (Rig Veda 3.62.10) in howItsDone; confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): 'curly hair' corrected to the child's side-locks (kakapaksha) and 'ten days' to the text's ten nights; cut 'every king' and 'a scene every parent understands'; the old closing line said the father knew his son was ready, which the text contradicts (Dasharatha says Rama is not ready to fight); the practice no longer tells the listener what they feel.
